From Python, any channel of a recording is one call away without an exporter: v2xw.Recording.open(path).arrow("node.rx") (Python).

items.title: VeReMi traces
items.text:
The format the misbehaviour-detection literature reads: VeReMi (van der Heijden, Lukaseder, Kargl, SecureComm 2018) and the VeReMi Extension (Kamel et al., ICC 2020), so a detector written against them reads this engine's output unchanged. Field names are VeReMi's (rcvTime, sendTime, senderPseudo, messageID, pos, pos_noise, spd, spd_noise, acl, acl_noise, hed, hed_noise, RSSI, attackerType).

codebook Attack codes Files veremi-ext (default) the F2MD attack enumeration 0–19 traceJSON-<rx>-<module>-A<code>-<t0>-<slice>.json per receiver and slice; traceGroundTruthJSON-<slice>.json veremi-1 VeReMi 1.0 bit codes: 1 ConstPos, 2 ConstPosOffset, 4 RandomPos, 8 RandomPosOffset, 16 EventualStop traceJSON-<receiver>.json per receiver; GroundTruthJSONlog.json

slice_s is the slice length (default 3600 s, F2MD's VeReMiSliceTime; 1 s to one week). An engine attack family gets a code only where its behaviour matches the codebook's attack; any other is code 1024, which a consumer can recognise rather than misread.

One deliberate deviation from VeReMi

VeReMi's per-receiver sender field holds the transmitter's real module id, a ground-truth column inside a receiver-visible file that lets a detector link every pseudonym for free. This exporter writes sender as a stable integer derived from the pseudonym; the true identity is only in the ground-truth file. The written traces go through the leakage linter, and the export fails if it finds anything.

Naming veremi also makes every BSM's node.tx record carry the broadcast position accuracy and acceleration that pos_noise and acl are read from; a run without it records exactly what it did before.

items.title: SUMO output files
items.text:
Each writes the file SUMO's option of the same name would, readable by SUMO's tools. They need a full recording (they read gt.kinematics), and naming one makes the run record gt.spawn and gt.despawn.

id File SUMO equivalent Options (default) sumo-fcd fcd.xml --fcd-output period_s (every step), precision (2) sumo-tripinfo tripinfo.xml --tripinfo-output write_unfinished (false), precision sumo-edgedata edgedata.xml <edgeData> period_s (whole run), precision sumo-lanedata lanedata.xml <laneData> period_s, precision sumo-summary summary.xml --summary-output period_s (every step), precision sumo-e1 e1.xml <inductionLoop> detectors: [{id, lane, pos_m}] (required; lane a SUMO lane id), period_s, precision sumo-e2 e2.xml <laneAreaDetector> detectors: [{id, lane, pos_m, length_m}], period_s, time_threshold_s (1), speed_threshold_mps (1.39), jam_threshold_m (10), precision

To export the network and demand themselves (not outputs), use v2xw export-sumo.

items.title: Dataset profiles and the release schema
items.text:
v2xw_record::dataset holds the dataset writers: the ma-dataset profile (two schema versions), receiver-logs, telemetry and net-trace, a DATASHEET.md writer and the leakage linter that gates all of them. Every write goes through two gates: floats are put on their declared grids and scanned back, and the linter inspects the node-visible files on disk and refuses to finish if identity or labels leak into them, with the verdict recorded in the datasheet.

Reachability in this build

These profiles are library writers over a finished recording. They are not ids of the scenario's exporters list, and the live server's export.dataset method answers that it does not host them. The exporters above are what v2xw run writes.

The public release schema, with its local (each vehicle's OBU), global (the Misbehaviour Authority) and truth views, is specified in Dataset schema. That page is a draft: it states what the engine must gain before the release is exported.

items.title: Experiments and sweeps
items.text:
An experiment block turns one scenario into a study: a factorial sweep over scenario fields, a list of seed slots and a replication count. v2xw experiment expands it into runs, executes them, pools each run's metrics, aggregates across replications with confidence intervals and writes one results table, journalling as it goes so an interruption costs only the run in flight. Code: crates/v2xw-experiment.

scenarios/revocation-latency.yaml (excerpt)
experiment:
  sweep:
    actors.vehicles.demand.rate_veh_per_h: [1500.0, 6000.0, 24000.0]
    threats.attackers[0].fraction: [0.02, 0.10]
  seeds: [1, 2, 3]
  replications: 1

Three rates × two attacker fractions × three seed slots × one replication is 18 runs.

Field Meaning sweep dotted path (a.b[0].c indexes a list) → the values to try; the axes' cross product is the set of cells seeds seed slots: each declared value is mixed with the master seed, not used as the seed replications runs per (cell, seed slot)

A swept path must already exist

A sweep replaces a value in the serialised scenario, and an optional field left unset is not serialised. Set every swept field in the base file (as the study files do for actors.vehicles.demand.rate_veh_per_h, security.pseudonym_change.period_s and threats.attackers[0].fraction), or the plan is refused.

items.title: The plan
items.text:
flowchart LR
  B[experiment block] --> P[ExperimentPlan::expand]
  P --> C["cells: cross product of the axes<br/>(last axis fastest)"]
  C --> R["runs: cell × seed slot × replication<br/>id c0000-s00-r000"]
  R --> X[execute, serially by default]
  X --> J[(journal.jsonl)]
  X --> M[run-metrics.json per run]
  M --> A[aggregate per cell and metric]
  A --> T[(results.json, .parquet / .arrow / .jsonl)]

The expansion is a pure function: it draws nothing, reads no clock and touches no file, so the same block always yields the same runs in the same order.

  • Axis order is the sweep's key order, which is lexicographic in the dotted path whatever order the YAML used.
  • Cell order is an odometer with the last axis varying fastest.
  • Run order within a cell is seed slot, then replication. A run's id is c<cell>-s<slot>-r<replication>.

Seeds are derived, never drawn:

\[ \text{seed} = \mathrm{SHA\text{-}256}(\texttt{"v2xw/experiment/seed/1"} \parallel m \parallel s \parallel d \parallel r)[0..8] \]

with \(m\) the master seed, \(s\) the slot index, \(d\) the declared slot value and \(r\) the replication, read as a little-endian u64. The cell index is deliberately not an input: every cell uses the same seed for the same (slot, replication), which is common random numbers. Two protocols compared at slot 3 ran on the same arrivals, fading draws and attacker decisions, so their difference is not inflated by between-run variance. Mixing in the master seed keeps two experiments that both chose [1, 2, 3] from sharing streams.

items.title: Running a sweep
items.text:
v2xw experiment status scenarios/pdr-vs-distance.yaml --out runs/pdr    # the plan, nothing run
v2xw experiment run    scenarios/pdr-vs-distance.yaml --out runs/pdr --format parquet
v2xw experiment resume scenarios/pdr-vs-distance.yaml --out runs/pdr    # after an interruption

experiment      pdr-vs-distance
plan            544d30e4…
outputs         runs/pdr
sweep           2 cell(s) x 5 seed slot(s) x 1 replication(s)

journal         none — this sweep has not been started here
progress        0 of 10 run(s) done, 10 outstanding
next
  c0000-s00-r000
  c0000-s01-r000
  …

Flags (--concurrency, --ci, --no-recording, --node-only, --no-verify, --keyframe-ms, --build-utc, --format): v2xw experiment. The manifest timestamp is read once and shared by every run, so two runs of one cell differ in their seed and nothing else.

Serial by default

--concurrency defaults to 1 (runner::DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY). Each concurrent run holds its own world, scheduler, node state and recording buffer, so k runs cost k times the peak memory of one, and the engine already uses the machine's cores inside a single run. Raise it only on a machine with memory to spare.

The journal. journal.jsonl is append-only, one line per finished run, flushed before the runner moves on, keyed by run id. Its header carries the plan digest (SHA-256 of the sweep's canonical JSON), so a changed sweep is refused rather than mixed into the old table. run skips whatever the journal says is done; resume additionally refuses when no journal for this plan exists. Each entry's wall-clock time is a measurement, never part of the results.

items.title: Outputs
items.text:
runs/pdr/
├── experiment.json          the expanded plan
├── journal.jsonl            what has finished
├── results.json             the results table, with its plan digest
├── results.parquet          with --format parquet (or .arrow, .jsonl)
└── runs/
    └── c0000-s00-r000/
        ├── scenario.yaml        the materialised scenario of this run
        ├── run-metrics.json     this run's metrics reduced to one value per metric per bin
        ├── metrics.json, run-report.json, manifest.json
        └── recording.mcap       unless --no-recording

items.title: From windows to one value per run
items.text:
A run emits a sample per metric, per dimension bin, per window. reduce pools the windows first, so a window of four trials and one of four thousand are not weighted alike:

Sample shape Pooled across windows proportion (pdr, det_recall, …) successes and trials added; the interval is computed once, over the real trial count ratio of sums (cbr, envelope_overhead, …) numerators and denominators added scalar the windows' points averaged distribution the windows' means averaged count added

items.title: From runs to a row
items.text:
aggregate turns a cell's replications into one row per metric and bin, carrying replications, replications_with_value, samples, mean, ci_lo, ci_hi, ci_level, ci_method, stddev, min, max and per_replication.

ci_method When Interval wilson a proportion the Wilson score interval over the pooled successes and trials, computed by v2xw-metrics normal-over-replications anything else, with at least two replications \(\bar x \pm z\, s/\sqrt{k}\) over the \(k\) replications' values none fewer than two usable replications, or a pooled proportion the metric calls insufficient no interval: the mean is a fact about one run, not an estimate

The normal approximation

With \(k\) below about thirty, \(z\,s/\sqrt k\) is narrower than a Student-\(t\) interval. The row carries replications and stddev beside the interval so a reader can see what it is worth and recompute it under another rule.

items.title: The MA policy family
items.text: A sweep over security.scms.ma_policy.preset additionally writes ma-policy-family.csv and ma-policy-family.md: one row per (policy, seed) and a mean with a 95 % interval per policy. The interval here is Student's \(t\) over the seeds, \(\bar x \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt n\), because with two or three seeds the normal quantile would overstate the precision. Every point is a full run, so unlike v2xw ma-replay --policies it includes the feedback (revoked devices stop sending, CRL delays apply). Ground truth is joined only after every run has decided.

items.title: Figures
items.text:
v2xw_experiment::figures turns a results table into Plotly figure JSON from declared presets (rq-pdr-distance, rq-density-congestion, rq-pseudonym-privacy, rq-revocation-latency, rq-rat-comparison, rq-insider-detection, rq-vertical-slice). It is a library API; there is no v2xw figure command:

use v2xw_experiment::figures::{preset, render};
let spec = preset("rq-pdr-distance").expect("a known preset");
for file in render(&spec, &table).write(std::path::Path::new("runs/pdr/figures"))? {
    println!("{file}");
}

A panel whose metric has no provider in this build says so on the figure instead of drawing an empty axis.

items.title: The foundry
items.text: v2xw_experiment::foundry is a MAP-Elites quality-diversity search over scenario space for the cases a detector misses: one elite per descriptor cell (attack family, density band, topology, attacker band, RAT, protocol), so the archive is a map of where a fixed detector fails. Mutations touch only adversary, environment and topology settings, never detection.*, security.verification_policy or a detector threshold, and an injected operator is held to the same list. An elite replays as a scenario file plus a seed. It is a library API over the same run executor (foundry::search), writing archive.json and FOUNDRY_REPORT.md; foundry_eval checks whether a proposed mutation operator beats random search.

items.title: Study files that ship with a sweep
items.text:
File Sweep Runs pdr-vs-distance.yaml propagation tier × 5 seeds 10 density-sweep-congestion.yaml 5 demand rates × 3 seeds 15 pseudonym-privacy.yaml 4 pseudonym periods × 3 seeds 12 pseudonym-strategies.yaml 5 pseudonym-change strategies 5 revocation-latency.yaml 3 demand rates × 2 attacker fractions × 3 seeds 18 glosa-energy.yaml GLOSA compliance × 3 seeds 9 rat-comparison.yaml radio technology × 5 seeds 15 pq-signatures.yaml 7 signature schemes 7 pq-full-stack.yaml 3 KEMs × 2 signatures 6 pq-certificate-cycle.yaml 2 fragmenters × 2 seeds 4 threshold-pca.yaml 3 threshold protocols 3

Each states at the top what it measures and what it does not. For a ladder of one parameter, a set of overlay files (meta.base) is the alternative to a sweep: each is its own scenario with its own hash and runs under the file's seed, while a sweep's cells share the derived seeds of their slots (Scenarios).

items.title: Running and recording
items.text:
A run is a scenario, a seed and an engine build. There are two ways to drive one: v2xw run from the command line, which runs to the end and writes a run directory, and the engine server, which streams the run to the Studio and takes control calls. Both execute the same engine and the same event loop (Architecture).

flowchart LR
  A[v2xw run] --> E[Engine::build + run]
  B["v2xw-server / v2xw serve<br/>run.start, run.pause, run.seek…"] --> E
  E --> R["recorder (record level, profile)"]
  R --> M[(recording.mcap or segments)]
  E --> MP[metric providers] --> J[metrics.json]
  E --> RR[run-report.json, manifest.json]
  M --> V[read back and verify]

items.title: v2xw run
items.text:
v2xw run scenarios/attack-fake-positions.yaml --out runs/attack
v2xw run scenarios/midtown-normal.yaml --city seattle --duration 15m --build-utc 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z

Every flag with its default: v2xw run. The scenario is loaded, the city and overrides applied, and then validated, so the checked scenario is the one that runs (an override that pushes a timeline event past the end is refused).

Override Scenario field Notes --duration 15m, --duration-s 900 time.duration_s --duration wins --rate-veh-per-h N actors.vehicles.demand.rate_veh_per_h no effect when the scenario states a per-lane-km rate --city ID city, world moves roadside units, rescales demand (what changes) --veremi veremi-ext\|veremi-1 exporters adds or sets the VeReMi exporter (Datasets)

Each override changes the scenario hash and is in scenario.resolved.yaml. --build-utc fixes the manifest timestamp, the only clock reading on this path; pass it when two manifests must compare field by field.

items.title: What a run writes
items.text:
File Contents Reproducible recording.mcap every record and VWP frame, the manifest metadata, the resolved scenario attached its data section is; its file hash is not scenario.resolved.yaml the scenario after overlay merge, migration, defaults and overrides yes metrics.json every metric.sample yes run-report.json event, frame and record counts per channel; content_digest yes manifest.json build hash, engine and crate versions, every model with its card hash, world, scenario and seed, crypto mode, the files above digested all but build_utc and the recording's file hash progress.jsonl one line per progress interval (empty when there is none) no: wall-clock measurements checkpoint.json, recording.NNNN.mcap, recording_index.json with --checkpoint-every the segments' contents are <exporter>/ one directory per named exporter (Datasets and exports) yes

The digest to compare is content_digest: SHA-256 over every message's topic, log time and bytes in stored order. The MCAP writer emits its summary index in hash-map order, so recording.mcap's own SHA-256 may differ between two identical runs; v2xw run prints both. Channels, encodings and the manifest fields: Recording format.

items.title: Recording levels
items.text:
--record-level decides which records reach the recording. Metrics are computed in the engine from the full record stream at every level, so metrics.json is the same.

Level Keeps Use full (default) every record and the snapshot stream (vwp/keyframe, vwp/delta) the Studio replays it; check-traffic and energy need it (gt.kinematics) receptions every record, no snapshot frames, no gt.kinematics per-reception analysis at about a third of the size events drops the per-reception journals node.rx, phy.rx, node.verify (they grow with the square of the fleet) and gt.kinematics attack and backend studies with many vehicles metrics metric samples and summary records only: scenario events, MA decisions and cases, revocations, spawns and despawns, credential milestones runs of days

Other ways to make a recording smaller or blind:

Flag Effect --node-only the NODE-only profile: every ground-truth record is refused and in the snapshot frames an unequipped actor's slot is empty and lanes and the attacker flag are blanked --no-recording no file at all; with --digest the record stream is still hashed (stream_digest) so two runs can be compared bit for bit --keyframe-ms the keyframe period (a whole number of mobility steps): seek granularity against size --attach-world adds the world payload (tens of MB for a city); off by default time.metric_period_s metric window length (1 s when unset); a minute's period writes a sixtieth of the samples time.warmup_s windows that end inside the warm-up are not sampled

For scale: the 60-second scenarios/phase1-grid.yaml (one or two vehicles) writes a recording of about 0.55 MB at full. Size grows with the fleet, and the per-reception journals with its square, which is what the coarser levels are for.

items.title: Long runs: progress, checkpoint, resume
items.text:
v2xw run scenarios/manhattan-day.yaml --out runs/day \
    --record-level metrics --checkpoint-every 1h --progress-every 30m
# … interrupted …
v2xw resume runs/day/checkpoint.json
  • Progress. Every --progress-every (default 15 minutes of simulated time for runs of an hour or more), a JSON line goes to progress.jsonl and a short line to stderr: the simulated instant, wall clock for the slice, memory footprint and the engine's collection sizes. --quiet keeps the file and silences stderr. None of it reaches a digest.
  • Checkpoint. Every --checkpoint-every, the open recording segment is finished and the next opened (recording.0000.mcap, recording.0001.mcap, … listed in recording_index.json), and checkpoint.json (format v2xw-checkpoint/1) records the scenario and world hashes, build timestamp, the instant, the record digest and count at that instant, and how much of each output was complete. Each segment is a complete recording that v2xw info and the Studio open.
  • Resume. v2xw resume rebuilds the engine from scenario.resolved.yaml, replays to the checkpoint with outputs off, refuses to continue unless the record digest matches, cuts the outputs back to the checkpoint and carries on. The finished outputs equal an uninterrupted run's.

What a checkpoint does not store

It does not serialise the engine's memory; resuming re-simulates the time before the checkpoint without recording it. What it saves is everything written before the checkpoint and the proof that the resumed run is the same run.

v2xw-server --resume <checkpoint.json> serves a checkpointed run paused at the checkpoint's instant, for inspection in the Studio.

items.title: Verification and v2xw info
items.text: After a run the recording is read back unless --no-verify (or --no-recording): every record and frame is walked, the content digest computed and each chunk's CRC checked. The summary line says integrity VERIFIED only when every chunk carried a checksum and it matched. v2xw info runs the same walk on any recording and prints the manifest, the channels with their visibility class and counts, and the attachments (first simulation, step 5).

items.title: Running under the server
items.text:
v2xw-server and v2xw serve hold one run and stream it over WebSocket (/vwp/v1) while taking JSON-RPC calls on the socket and on POST /rpc. Run control:

Method Parameters Does run.start scenario (path or document), city, seed, speed (0–100), paused, record (default true), record_path, label load a scenario and begin the stream; returns run id, state, world and scenario hashes run.pause / run.resume pause at the next mobility-step boundary after flushing every frame; resume run.step unit (step, event, keyframe, second), count (1–100,000) advance a paused run run.seek t_ns, fraction or event; pause_after (default true) reposition; the keyframe and deltas arrive before the reply. Outside the produced range it fails with -32003, whose data carries the range that works run.speed speed (multiple of real time, 0 unthrottled), sync (free, client) pacing run.stop finalize_exports (default true) stop and finalise outputs; returns the recording path and digest run.status state, position, end, speed, profile, live, actor and node counts export.recording path, time range, channels, profile (full, node), compression copy part of the recording, optionally stripped to the node profile 
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8787/rpc -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"run.status","params":{}}'

How far back run.seek can go is bounded by the server's --retain (mobility steps, default 36,000) and --retain-mb (default 1,024 MB). Every method, its errors and the stream frames: Engine server and RPC and VWP v1.

./run-sim.sh [scenario] is the shortcut for the Studio: it builds v2xw-server if needed and starts it paused, unthrottled, on $V2XW_PORT (default 8787), reading the assistant's variables from .env.

items.title: Sensitivity analysis
items.text:
v2xw sensitivity asks of a parameter: does it move the metric theory says it moves, in the direction theory says? Every check runs a base scenario and a changed one on the same seed. Same seed is common random numbers: the two runs draw the same vehicles, phases and fading wherever the change does not reach, so a small effect is not lost in run-to-run noise, and a setting the run never reads gives a bit-identical run. Code: crates/v2xw-engine/src/sensitivity.rs and sensitivity/{sweep,expect}.rs.

Mode Command What runs spec v2xw sensitivity <spec.yaml> the rows of one spec file, each a one-at-a-time change on its base catalogue v2xw sensitivity --catalogue every published numeric and choice setting, at each end of its recommended range expectations v2xw sensitivity --expect only the perturbations the expectation table names, plus the two-setting interaction checks

Every flag: v2xw sensitivity.

items.title: Spec files
items.text:
a spec file
base: ../scenarios/sensitivity/dsrc-grid.yaml   # relative to this file
set: { time.duration_s: 3.0 }                   # applied to every run
rows:
  - name: lower transmit power
    set: { radio.devices.obu.tx_power_dbm: 5.0 }
    metric: range_m
    expect: down          # up | down | same | changes
    band: [0.2, 0.8]      # optional: changed / base must fall in it
    min_change: 0.05      # optional: relative change required (default 0.01)
    base_set: { }         # optional: fields applied to both runs of this row
    source: Friis / log-distance law
Row field Meaning name the row's label set the dotted fields this row changes metric the measured metric to judge expect up, down, same or changes band optional [lo, hi] the ratio changed / base must fall in, where theory gives one min_change relative change that counts as a move (default 0.01) base_set fields applied to both runs, so the row is measured where the setting acts source the theory or citation the expectation rests on

The metrics are measured while the run goes, from phy.prr, node.tx, node.rx, mac.cbr and the run report, as running sums and histograms (never the records, so a large fleet does not hold its phy.rx stream in memory): PDR and PRR, the range edges range_m and range90_m, PRR per distance band (prr_0_200, prr_200_400, prr_400_600, prr_600_1000), CBR, latency stages, age of information and inter-packet gap.

v2xw sensitivity scenarios/sensitivity/radio-dsrc.yaml                 # PASS/FAIL per row on stderr, a table on stdout
v2xw sensitivity scenarios/sensitivity/radio-dsrc.yaml --base-only     # every metric of the base, and its PRR curve in 20 m bins
v2xw sensitivity scenarios/sensitivity/radio-dsrc.yaml --markdown out/radio.md --json

The command exits 1 when a row does not move as expected. Shipped spec files in scenarios/sensitivity/: radio-dsrc.yaml, radio-dsrc-dense.yaml, radio-cv2x.yaml, radio-gn.yaml, phy-channel.yaml, test-mac-congestion.yaml, test-mac-congestion-sidelink.yaml, test-networking.yaml, test-networking-dsrc.yaml. The same rows run as tests in crates/v2xw-engine/tests/sensitivity_*.rs.

items.title: The catalogue sweep
items.text:
v2xw sensitivity --catalogue --plan                          # settings, values and families; runs nothing
v2xw sensitivity --catalogue --only radio.phy,radio.mac --jobs 2 --cache out/sens.jsonl
v2xw sensitivity --catalogue --cache out/sens.jsonl --markdown out/catalogue.md --strict

The settings come from the engine's published settings index (scenario::publish::fields), the same index the Studio's settings window and the assistant read, so a field added to the schema is swept with no edit here. Each setting is moved to the low and high end of its recommended range (parsed from its guide text and kept inside the validator's bound), else half and twice its default; a choice to its other values (at most max_choices); a switch to its other value.

flowchart LR
  F[published settings] --> P[plan: low and high end per setting]
  FAM[families file] --> P
  P --> R["route to a family by prefix<br/>(retry the next family if refused)"]
  R --> RUN[run on the family base, same seed]
  RUN --> FP["fingerprint: ~250-300 metrics"]
  FP --> D{equals the base?}
  D -- yes --> DEAD[dead setting]
  D -- no --> E[compare with expectation rows]
  E --> V[agrees / contradicted]

Each run is measured into a fingerprint: the radio harness's metrics, every numeric leaf of the run report (report.*), the sample-weighted mean of every metric sample (metric.*) and the ground-truth traffic state (traffic.*, vru.*).

Result Meaning dead the fingerprint equals the base's: the setting is not read, or read by nothing a metric observes, on that family. Same seed means this needs no tolerance contradiction an expectation row disagrees with the measured direction or size refused every family's loader rejected the perturbation (usually by design: a setting that needs a partner setting)

--cache FILE keeps a JSON-lines record of finished perturbations; a rerun reuses every entry whose setting, value and family scenarios match, so a stopped sweep resumes and only changed entries re-run. --strict exits 1 on a contradiction.

items.title: The families file
items.text:
scenarios/sensitivity/catalogue.yaml (--families) holds:

Key What it says families named small scenarios: {name, base, set}, for example dsrc (40 vehicles on a 1.2 km open grid, 802.11p, 2 s), cv2x, nr, gn, security, scms, traffic, saturated, osm, canyon, pedestrians, freeway, freight routes {prefix, families}: which families a setting runs on, first match wins; the last route ("") is the fallback skip {prefix, reason}: settings not swept (descriptive fields, the seed, the run length, settings that need a structure a scalar cannot supply) values literal values that replace the computed ends, where the range would make a run too large or names no usable range max_choices the most values a choice is swept at context {prefix, set}: prerequisites both runs share so a setting is measured where it acts (for example radio.channel_model.nakagami_shape with fading: nakagami)

The latest full catalogue run and how to read its tables: Sensitivity catalogue.

items.title: Expectations
items.text:
An expectation row encodes one piece of theory, with its citation, about one setting:

crates/v2xw-engine/tests/expectations/radio.yaml (excerpt)
- {setting: radio.devices.obu.antenna_gain_dbi, change: high, metric: prr, expect: up,
   source: "EIRP and receive gain add dB for dB to the link budget (Friis 1946; ETSI EN 302 571 EIRP limits)"}
- {setting: radio.channel_model.path_loss_exponent, change: high, metric: prr, expect: down,
   source: "log-distance law: 10 n log10(d) more loss (Rappaport 4.9; Cheng et al., IEEE JSAC 2007 measured n 2-4 for V2V)"}
Field Meaning setting the dotted setting change low or high (the ends the sweep computes), or a literal value metric a fingerprint name expect up, down, same or changes min_change relative change required (default 0.01) source the theory and its citation

Only physics and traffic theory with a citation goes in the table. The files are crates/v2xw-engine/tests/expectations/*.yaml by topic (radio, PHY and channel, MAC congestion, networking, security and SCMS, traffic flow, VRU safety, run cost, couplings). Every row and the theory behind each contradiction: Sensitivity expectations.

items.title: Interaction checks
items.text:
Two settings together, as a 2 × 2 factorial on one family with all four runs on the same seed: the base, the factor alone (A), the condition alone (B) and both (AB). The factor's effect without the condition, \(A - \text{base}\), is compared with its effect under it, \(AB - B\), in the metric's own units (Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments 9e, §5.2: the interaction is the difference between the simple effects).

crates/v2xw-engine/tests/expectations/interactions/interactions.yaml (excerpt)
- name: density x reactive DCC (CBR)
  family: dsrc
  base_set: {time.mobility_step_ms: 50, messages.rate_hz: 20.0}
  factor: {actors.vehicles.demand.params.max_total_vehicles: 160}
  condition: {radio.models.dcc: {id: dcc/etsi/reactive-ts102687, params: {}}}
  metric: cbr_mean
  expect: dampens
  direction: up
  source: "reactive DCC moves to a longer Toff as CBR crosses 0.30/0.40/0.50/0.60 … (ETSI TS 102 687 V1.2.1 Table A.2)"
expect Holds when dampens the effect under the condition is smaller in size (it may vanish) amplifies it is larger in size, the same way holds it keeps its sign reverses it changes sign

direction is the factor's effect alone, checked too.

v2xw sensitivity --expect --plan                     # rows, perturbations, interactions, anything unplanned
v2xw sensitivity --expect --jobs 2 --cache out/expect.jsonl --markdown out/expect.md

--expect exits 1 when a row or an interaction fails, or when a row names a setting and end the sweep cannot plan. crates/v2xw-engine/tests/sensitivity_catalogue.rs is the fast CI subset: it checks that every expectation names a plannable setting and end, and that a few link-budget and frame settings on the DSRC family move the way the table says.

items.title: Writing a new expectation
items.text:
1. Find the setting's path and recommended range in the configuration reference.
  2. Check which family it routes to (--catalogue --plan --only <path>); add a route or a context if no family exercises it.
  3. Add a row with the theory and its citation to the topic file, and run v2xw sensitivity --expect --only <path>.
  4. If the run contradicts it, either the expectation or the engine is wrong; the contradiction table in Sensitivity expectations is where each one is explained.

items.title: SUMO co-simulation
items.text:
Eclipse SUMO and this engine meet in four places (crates/v2xw-interop):

Direction What How SUMO → engine a SUMO network as the world world.source.kind: sumo-net (Worlds and maps) SUMO → engine SUMO route files as demand driven by this engine's mobility actors.vehicles.demand.kind: mobility/demand/sumo-rou SUMO ↔ engine SUMO drives the traffic over TraCI while this engine runs radio, security, backend and UI mobility.provider: sumo engine → SUMO the world and demand in SUMO formats; SUMO-format outputs v2xw export-sumo; the sumo-* exporters (Datasets)

items.title: Finding SUMO
items.text:
SUMO is found through mobility.sumo_home, else $SUMO_HOME, else the sumo directory of the eclipse-sumo Python wheel in the virtualenv $V2XW_SUMO_VENV (<venv>/lib/python3.*/site-packages/sumo):

python3 -m venv ~/sumo-venv && ~/sumo-venv/bin/pip install eclipse-sumo
export V2XW_SUMO_VENV=~/sumo-venv          # or SUMO_HOME=/path/to/sumo

just sumo-install prints the install options (brew install --cask sumo-gui on macOS, or uv pip install eclipse-sumo libsumo). Nothing else in the engine needs SUMO: the shipped-scenario suites run without it, which is why the TraCI scenarios live in scenarios/interop/.

items.title: The TraCI tier (mobility.provider: sumo)
items.text:
scenarios/interop/sumo-grid.yaml (excerpt)
world:
  source: {kind: sumo-net, path: worlds/sumo/grid3.net.xml}
  imported_at: "2026-10-07T00:00:00Z"
mobility:
  provider: sumo
  route_files: [worlds/sumo/grid3.rou.xml]     # SUMO reads and routes these itself
  # sumo_args: [--default.carfollowmodel, IDM]
actors:
  vehicles:
    demand:
      kind: mobility/demand/poisson            # also applies: routed here, inserted into SUMO
      rate_veh_per_h_per_lane_km: 20.0
Setting Meaning mobility.provider native (default) or sumo mobility.route_files .rou.xml files SUMO loads and routes itself mobility.sumo_args extra SUMO command-line options mobility.sumo_home SUMO's installation directory (holding bin/sumo)

The world must be the net.xml SUMO runs: the importer keeps each SUMO edge id as the edge name and each lane's index, so a SUMO lane id is always a world lane and the reverse, without geometric matching.

sequenceDiagram
  participant E as engine (model id mobility/sumo-traci)
  participant S as sumo --remote-port
  E->>S: launch with the scenario seed, single thread
  loop every mobility step
    E->>S: route.add + vehicle.add for this engine's new trips
    E->>S: simulationStep(dt)
    S-->>E: per vehicle: front-bumper position, speed, angle, acceleration, lane (one batched message)
    E->>E: convert frame and reference point, publish as ground truth
    E->>E: radio, signing, verification, backend, detection, stream
  end

What SUMO owns: every vehicle's motion: car following, lane changing, junction behaviour and its own signal programmes.

What the engine owns: everything else: messages, radio, network, security, the credential system, attackers, detectors, metrics and the stream to the Studio, all computed on SUMO's published states.

The frame conversion. SUMO publishes the front bumper and an angle in degrees clockwise from north; this engine publishes the rear reference point and a heading counter-clockwise from east, so \(h = \pi/2 - \text{angle}\cdot\pi/180\) and \(\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_\text{front} - L(\cos h, \sin h)\), after the importer's shift.

Determinism. SUMO is deterministic for a fixed --seed and one simulation thread; the engine passes the scenario seed, sorts what it publishes by actor id, and assigns actor ids in sorted SUMO-id order of first appearance, so two runs with the same seed publish the same states.

items.title: What is and is not synchronised
items.text: Synchronised Not synchronised (from the model card's limitations) vehicle position, speed, heading, acceleration and lane, every step signal states: SUMO runs its own programme and does not publish it back; SPaT the engine generates follows the world's plan, which is the same programme only when SUMO's tlLogic was imported unchanged this engine's demand, inserted into SUMO on this engine's routes vehicles inside a junction are on SUMO internal lanes, which the world folds into connectors; their lane position is left empty there SUMO-routed vehicles from route_files pedestrians and SUMO persons are not read

items.title: SUMO route files driven natively (mobility/demand/sumo-rou)
items.text:
A .rou.xml driven by this engine's own mobility, with no SUMO install:

scenarios/interop/sumo-rou-native.yaml (excerpt)
actors:
  vehicles:
    demand:
      kind: mobility/demand/sumo-rou
      params:
        path: worlds/sumo/grid3-calibrated.rou.xml
        probability_flows: bernoulli        # or equal-spacing

Read: <vType> (vClass, maxSpeed, accel, decel, tau, minGap, sigma, speedFactor including norm/normc, speedDev, desiredMaxSpeed, probability), <vTypeDistribution>, <routeDistribution>, <route>, <vehicle>, <trip> and <flow>. Flows with vehsPerHour, period or number are equally spaced as in SUMO; period="exp(λ)" draws exponential headways; probability p is a Bernoulli trial every second (SUMO's definition; equal-spacing keeps the mean and drops the variance). departLane, departPos and departSpeed keywords that need the occupancy at insertion fall back to the nearest supported meaning and are counted as approximations. Every other attribute and <param> is counted by name in the import ledger, never dropped silently. A vehicle with a route drives exactly the file's edges.

items.title: Exporting to SUMO
items.text:
v2xw export-sumo scenarios/phase1-grid.yaml --out out/sumo
File What <stem>.nod.xml junctions: traffic_light when signalised, allway_stop, priority, right_before_left <stem>.edg.xml edges with lanes, speeds, widths and allowed classes (spreadType="right") <stem>.con.xml permitted lane-to-lane connections <stem>.net.xml when netconvert is found ($SUMO_HOME, $V2XW_SUMO_VENV) <stem>.rou.xml every trip the scenario's demand draws over the run, with this engine's route

Signal programmes are not exported

netconvert generates its default programme for each traffic_light node, so a SUMO run on an exported world has the same signalised junctions and different timings. Junction internals are left to netconvert. A world that came from a net.xml keeps its SUMO edge ids, so its .rou.xml runs on the original network unchanged: run SUMO on that file, not on an export.

items.title: Cross-validation
items.text: cross_validate (just cross-validate, --quick for shorter runs) compares traffic on a grid and on Midtown with SUMO, and radio against Veins and OpenCV2X. For traffic it runs the same trips through both simulators: the network is SUMO's (netgenerate --grid, and netconvert on the Midtown extract), one trip list is routed once by this engine's free-flow Dijkstra, and both drive those routes, so differences are in the driving models, not in routing. Both runs are measured by the same observer (Edie's generalised flow, density and speed, among others) and the report is written to target/validation/cross-validation.md. It needs SUMO. Scope and results: Validation and conformance tools.

items.title: Traffic demand
items.text:
Demand says when vehicles enter the world, where they start and end, and which way they go. It fills one slot, actors.vehicles.demand:

actors:
  vehicles:
    equipped_fraction: 1.0
    demand:
      kind: mobility/demand/poisson       # which demand model
      rate_veh_per_h: 1500.0              # or rate_veh_per_h_per_lane_km, or fleet_size
      params: {}                          # the model's own parameters
Field Meaning kind the demand model's id; default mobility/demand/none (nothing arrives) rate_veh_per_h vehicles per hour offered to the network rate_veh_per_h_per_lane_km the same as a density, multiplied by the built world's driving-lane length; wins over rate_veh_per_h, and is what makes a scenario fit any city fleet_size hold exactly this many vehicles on the road: a trip that ends is replaced, and the rate is not used params the model's parameter struct; unknown keys are refused at load

The vehicle mix, driver behaviour, GNSS and the other vehicle settings are in the actors reference; pedestrians and cyclists are actors.vru.

items.title: The demand kinds
items.text:
kind Arrivals params mobility/demand/poisson (alias …/poisson-thinned) a thinned Poisson process with a time-of-day shape the Poisson struct below, plus an optional od object mobility/demand/tr36885-drop one placement of vehicles along every lane, spaced by 3GPP TR 36.885 Table A.1.2-1 or TR 37.885 §6.1.2 variant, mean_gap_time, speeds, … mobility/demand/sumo-rou a SUMO .rou.xml: vTypes, routes, flows {path, probability_flows: bernoulli \| equal-spacing} mobility/demand/routes a v2xw/routes/1 file (an assignment's or a count sampler's output) {path} mobility/demand/trips a v2xw/trips/1 file, optionally assigned at load {path, assign?} mobility/demand/od-matrix an OD matrix turned into trips {matrix \| cells \| gravity, zones, od2trips?, assign?} mobility/demand/counts routes and trips that reproduce observed link counts {counts, sampler?, candidates?} mobility/demand/gtfs timetabled buses and street-level rail the transit struct below mobility/demand/purposes a day of home-based tours by trip purpose {daily_trips, purposes?, run_start_s_of_day?, seed?} mobility/demand/composite several of the above at once {parts: [{kind, params, rate_veh_per_h?}], utc_offset_s?} mobility/demand/none nothing

Paths are read relative to the working directory, as world.source.path is. Times of day are local: utc_offset_s (for example -28800 for Pacific standard time) turns the scenario's UTC time.t0 into the local start time that timetables, matrices and profiles are written in.

items.title: Poisson arrivals
items.text:
mobility/demand/poisson is an exact simulation of an inhomogeneous Poisson process by thinning: candidates arrive at a boosted constant rate and each is kept with the probability the time-of-day shape gives.

\[ \Delta t \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda\, b), \qquad P(\text{keep at } t) = \frac{m(f)}{b}, \qquad f = \frac{t}{T} \]

with \(\lambda\) the base rate, \(b \ge \sup m\) the candidate boost (candidate_boost) and \(T\) the run length. Shapes (profile):

profile \(m(f)\) uniform (default) \(1\) rush \(0.2 + 0.8\,\min\!\left(1,\ e^{-((f-0.25)/0.09)^2} + e^{-((f-0.75)/0.09)^2}\right)\): two peaks, a quiet midday night \(0.15 + 0.25 f\)

These shapes follow the fraction of the run, whatever its length. A run of hours or days uses daily instead: a factor for each hour of the local civil day, interpolated between hour centres, with weekday and weekend curves. The shipped curve (nyc-dot-manhattan, or -weekday/-weekend on every day) is NYC DOT's Automated Traffic Volume Counts for Manhattan, 2015 to 2026, normalised so the weekday factors average 1 (night lull 0.26 at 03:00, morning peak 1.30 at 08:00, evening plateau 1.33). rate_veh_per_h is then the mean weekday rate. The curve is a borough average, not the counts at the streets of a world, and the clock is standard time from a fixed UTC offset.

scenarios/manhattan-day.yaml (excerpt)
demand:
  kind: mobility/demand/poisson
  rate_veh_per_h: 300.0
  params:
    daily: {curve: nyc-dot-manhattan}     # utc_offset_h defaults from the world's longitude

Other Poisson parameters: max_total_vehicles (a cap, 0 for none), fleet (the class mix), speed (how a trip's desired speed is drawn; default SUMO-style class speed deviation), fleet_size, and od (where trips start and end: uniform or gravity destinations with w(h) = e^{−h/scale} over junction hops, optional perimeter origins). Every parameter with its source: mobility/demand/poisson-thinned.

The Studio's named rates for Midtown (crates/v2xw-engine/src/scenario/options.rs): Night 500, Light 1,500, Normal (midday) 3,000, Rush hour 4,500, Gridlock 9,000 veh/h. Their ratios are cited (HCM 6th ed. design-hour factor about 9 % of daily traffic; FHWA Traffic Monitoring Guide 2016, about 6 % at midday and 1 % in the small hours); their level is scaled to what the Midtown extract runs interactively.

Demand can also change during a run through the timeline: {t: 60.0, until: 240.0, type: demand.multiplier, value: 1.3} (events).

items.title: OD matrices
items.text:
demand:
  kind: mobility/demand/od-matrix
  params:
    zones: {kind: grid, cols: 2, rows: 2}
    cells:
      - {from: r0c0, to: r1c1, count: 120}
      - {from: r1c1, to: r0c0, count: 120}
    assign: {max_iterations: 4}
  • Formats (matrix: path): PTV VISUM/VISSIM O-format ($O, one from to count line per cell) and V-format ($V, a full square matrix), the two SUMO's od2trips reads, and a plain CSV from,to,count[,begin_s,end_s]. Or cells inline.
  • Synthesis (gravity): a doubly-constrained gravity model \(T_{ij} = a_i b_j P_i A_j f(c_{ij})\) balanced by Furness's method (Furness 1965; Ortúzar and Willumsen, Modelling Transport 4th ed., ch. 5), with exponential, power or combined deterrence. β is uncalibrated; the card gives Hyman's method (1969) to fit it.
  • Zones: a grid of the world (grid:CxR on the command line), weighted by building floor area.
  • Matrix to trips: each cell's count is scaled and rounded stochastically; departures are uniform in the interval or follow a departure profile; origin and destination lanes are drawn by zone weights. Draws are keyed by the cell, so changing one cell changes no other cell's trips.

items.title: Link counts
items.text:
A count is vehicles past a place in an interval. The place is an edge, a lane, or a real station's coordinate (with direction), snapped to the nearest road of matching heading:

id,kind,ref,begin_s,end_s,count
5th-ave-n,point,45.5190 -122.6765 0,0,3600,612
e17,edge,17,0,900,140

mobility/demand/counts builds routes and trips that reproduce them (max-entropy or greedy sampling). Any routed demand is checked against counts with the GEH statistic and the acceptance criterion of UK DfT TAG Unit M3.1 (2020) Table 2: GEH < 5 on at least 85 % of counts.

items.title: Route choice and dynamic traffic assignment
items.text:
assign (on od-matrix and trips, and the v2xw-demand assign command) runs an iterative dynamic traffic assignment in the manner of SUMO's duaIterate (Gawron 1998):

  1. every trip takes its free-flow time-dependent shortest path, or a saved assignment's;
  2. a network loader drives the routes and measures lane travel times per interval;
  3. the relative gap \(\sum (c_\text{used} - c_\text{best}) / \sum c_\text{used}\) is measured (Chiu et al., Dynamic Traffic Assignment: A Primer, TRB E-C153, 2011, §4);
  4. stop when the gap is below gap_tolerance (after min_iterations) or at max_iterations;
  5. otherwise the route-choice model updates each trip's probabilities, each trip draws its next route, and the loop repeats.
Route choice (assign.choice.model) Source gawron (default) Gawron 1998, pairwise update with smoothed costs; duarouter's default logit multinomial logit (Ben-Akiva and Lerman 1985) with the C-logit commonality correction (Cascetta et al. 1996) msa method of successive averages, 1/k onto the best route at iteration k (Sheffi 1985, ch. 12) Network loader (assign.loader.model) What it is queue (default) event-driven point queues with signal gating (Vickrey 1969), no spill-back bpr static link performance \(t = t_0 (1 + \alpha (v/c)^\beta)\) (Bureau of Public Roads 1964) micro the engine's own microscopic mobility driving the routes; most faithful, slowest

The result is a v2xw/routes/1 file: every trip with its alternatives, each route's cost and probability, the chosen one, the world hash it was made for, the parameters and the iteration log. mobility/demand/routes runs it. During a run, mobility/routing/dynamic-reroute re-plans at the next junction on a closure.

items.title: Trip purposes
items.text: mobility/demand/purposes generates a day as tours: a home-based tour leaves home at a time drawn from its purpose's departure profile, stays for a drawn duration and returns; non-home-based and commercial trips are single legs (purposes after NCHRP Report 716, ch. 4). Activities are drawn with distance decay \(w_j e^{-d_{ij}/d_0}\). The shipped purpose shares, profiles and durations are uncalibrated shapes, marked todo-calibrate with the plan of fitting the 2017 NHTS; a study passes its own per-purpose specification in purposes. Days are generated one at a time, keyed by (seed, day, purpose, tour), so a week costs one day's memory and a resumed run regenerates the same day.

items.title: Public transport (GTFS)
items.text:
scenarios/portland-transit.yaml (excerpt)
demand:
  kind: mobility/demand/composite
  params:
    utc_offset_s: -25200                  # 15:00 UTC is 08:00 Pacific daylight time
    parts:
      - kind: mobility/demand/poisson
        rate_veh_per_h: 1000.0
      - kind: mobility/demand/gtfs
        params:
          feed: worlds/cache/portland.gtfs
          date: 20261007
          dwell: {model: scheduled, min_s: 4.0}
          hold_early: true

The GTFS kind places each stop on the network, runs buses, trolleybuses and street-level rail (route types 0, 3, 5, 11, 700–799, 900–999 unless route_types says otherwise), with a dwell model and optional holding of early vehicles. Fetch and clip a feed, then check what the stop matcher made of it before running:

worlds/fetch.sh portland
worlds/fetch-gtfs.sh portland 20261007            # worlds/cache/portland.gtfs/
v2xw-demand gtfs --scenario scenarios/portland-transit.yaml \
    --feed worlds/cache/portland.gtfs --date 20261007 --start 08:00

items.title: The v2xw-demand tool
items.text:
Precomputes demand outside a run, against exactly the world a scenario builds, so the files' world hash matches when the scenario loads them. Every command and flag: Command-line tool.

v2xw-demand od2trips --scenario S.yaml --matrix city.od --zones grid:4x4 --start 07:00 --out trips.json
v2xw-demand assign   --scenario S.yaml --trips trips.json --choice logit --loader queue --out routes.json
v2xw-demand check    --scenario S.yaml --counts counts.csv --routes routes.json

assign prints one line per iteration (relative gap, mean travel time, arrivals, share switched, mean alternatives) and whether it converged. check prints observed and modelled counts with GEH per row and the TAG M3.1 verdict.

items.title: Adding a demand model
items.text: Implement v2xw_mobility::traits::Demand, add its id to v2xw_demand::scenario::KINDS and an arm to build; the engine forwards every kind in KINDS to that crate, so nothing in the engine changes. Each family (route choice, loader, dwell, deterrence, departure profile) has its own trait and spec enum, and each module ends with a "How to add another" note. See Extending: models.

items.title: Worlds and maps
items.text:
A world is everything that does not move: lanes, junctions with their connectors and conflict matrices, signal plans, crossings, buildings, terrain, vegetation, roadside sites, and a provenance record. v2xw-world builds it once per run, quantises it, hashes it (world_hash in the manifest) and every other crate reads it. A scenario gets its world one of three ways:

Way Scenario says Needs a city of the library city: <id>, or --city <id> the extract in worlds/cache/<id>.osm.xml an explicit source world.source: {kind: …} the file it names, or nothing for a procedural generator a city replacing the file's world v2xw run <scenario> --city <id> as the first row

Every world setting: world reference. The import models and their equations: Traffic and mobility.

items.title: The city library
items.text:
worlds/cities.yaml (schema v2xw/cities/1, compiled into the binary so every interface lists the same cities) holds the largest city of every US state and of DC, the most-studied connected-vehicle sites (the New York and Tampa USDOT pilots, Ann Arbor, Columbus, Pittsburgh, the large Texas and California cores) and Berlin-Mitte for the European stack. Each entry is a downtown box of about 1.5 km × 1.5 km:

Field Meaning id the city's name everywhere; its extract is worlds/cache/<id>.osm.xml bbox [south, west, north, east], WGS 84; its south-west corner is the world origin, so re-fetching cannot move a coordinate highway_preset the jurisdiction's default speed limits and rules of the road (crates/v2xw-world/src/jurisdiction.rs cites each) utc_offset_h standard-time offset fetched the download date, which becomes world.imported_at drive_lane_km, signals driving-lane length and signalised intersections, measured by city_audit; used to rescale demand 
v2xw cities                       # every city by state, [not fetched] where the extract is missing
v2xw cities --json                # the registry as JSON
worlds/fetch.sh boston            # one extract
worlds/fetch.sh --all             # every missing one (one at a time, FETCH_PAUSE_S apart)
worlds/fetch.sh --list            # ids and whether each extract is present
worlds/fetch.sh mytown 45.51,-122.69,45.53,-122.66   # any box: S,W,N,E

fetch.sh asks the Overpass API for every node and way in the box, the turn restrictions and the building multipolygons, leaves out far-reaching relations, retries with backoff, falls back to mirrors (OVERPASS_URL puts yours first) and rejects a truncated answer. V2XW_WORLDS_DIR points the engine at another extract directory.

items.title: What --city changes
items.text:
A scenario says what happens; a city says where (crates/v2xw-engine/src/city.rs). To make any scenario fit any city:

  1. The world. The city's extract, box, highway preset and fetch date go into world; the scenario's building and signal options stay.
  2. What belonged to the old city. Roadside units at explicit positions become an actors.rsu_placement of the same count and roles; a fixed arrival rate becomes a rate per kilometre of driving lane; the clock keeps its local time of day; a closure of a named street becomes target: auto; a focus box is dropped.
  3. The built world. Once imported, a per-lane-km rate becomes vehicles per hour and placed roadside units stand at the busiest signalised intersections (most approach lanes first, at least min_spacing_m apart).

So a scenario written with rate_veh_per_h_per_lane_km, rsu_placement, target: auto and at: busiest-junction runs on every city unchanged. Before a city is listed it is imported and run under the traffic auditor; a city that fails is listed under dropped: with the reason.

items.title: World sources
items.text:
world.source.kind selects the importer:

kind Reads Importer osm-xml path to a .osm/.osm.xml extract, optional bbox (min_lat_deg, min_lon_deg, max_lat_deg, max_lon_deg) world/source/osm sumo-net path to a SUMO net.xml world/source/sumo-net open-drive path to an ASAM OpenDRIVE .xodr, converted through netconvert world/source/opendrive procedural generator and params world/source/procedural-grid, -radial, -random

osm-bbox (fetch at load) and legacy-json are accepted by the type but have no importer in this build; a scenario naming them is refused with UnsupportedSource.

OpenStreetMapSUMO networkProcedural grid 
world:
  source:
    kind: osm-xml
    path: worlds/cache/manhattan.osm.xml
    bbox: {min_lat_deg: 40.744, min_lon_deg: -73.990, max_lat_deg: 40.762, max_lon_deg: -73.968}
  highway_preset: urban-us-nyc
  imported_at: "2026-09-18T00:00:00Z"

world:
  source: {kind: sumo-net, path: worlds/sumo/grid3.net.xml}
  imported_at: "2026-10-07T00:00:00Z"

world:
  source:
    kind: procedural
    generator: world/source/procedural-grid
    params: {cols: 13, rows: 34, block_x_m: 274.0, block_y_m: 80.0,
             lanes_per_direction: 2, signalised: true, cycle_s: 60.0,
             crossings: true, block_buildings: true}
  imported_at: "2026-09-18T00:00:00Z"

items.title: OpenStreetMap
items.text:
The importer builds drivable, pedestrian and cycle networks, junctions with connectors and conflict matrices, synthesised fixed-time signals, buildings with sourced heights, land-use zones and a provenance record. It needs a speed preset for roads with no maxspeed tag, and has no default: a fallback speed limit is a statement about a jurisdiction. Presets: urban-us-nyc, urban-us-portland, urban-de, sumo-german (netconvert's table, for comparability with SUMO), and an urban-us-<state> preset for every state (world.highway_preset).

OpenStreetMap carries no signal timing, so plans are synthesised; the world.signals block sets the cycle (default 90 s), all-red, pedestrian walk (7 s, MUTCD 2009 §4E.06) and walking speed (1.067 m/s), green-wave coordination and the joining of close junctions (netconvert's --tls.join). These apply to imported worlds only. world.service_roads keeps or drops highway=service alleys and driveways.

v2xw import-osm runs the same importer outside a run and writes the three world formats:

v2xw import-osm worlds/cache/portland.osm.xml out/portland --speed-preset urban-us-portland
File Format world.vwb the browser's binary vwp-world/1 payload (protocol §4) world.json the same payload as JSON world.v2xw the engine's native binary, an exact round trip (same content hash) report.txt what the importer kept, dropped and inferred, with every anomaly counted

The world validation report (geometry a car or pedestrian cannot use, every imported attribute against its source tags) runs as cargo run -p v2xw-world --example world_report -- <extract> --preset <p> [--baseline worlds/validation/<city>.json]; with --baseline it fails when a check's count rises above the committed ceiling.

items.title: SUMO net.xml and OpenDRIVE
items.text: sumo-net reads edges, lanes, junctions, connections, internal connectors, right-of-way matrices, traffic-light programmes and crossings into the same lane-level world, counting an anomaly wherever the formats disagree. Each SUMO edge id is kept as the edge's name, so a SUMO lane id is always a world lane, which is what the TraCI co-simulation relies on (SUMO co-simulation). world.sumo.signal_programmes runs actuated, delay-based and NEMA tlLogic as live controllers (as-file, the default) or flattens them (static). OpenDRIVE goes through netconvert, then the same reader.

items.title: Procedural networks
items.text:
Generator Shape Main parameters (defaults) world/source/procedural-grid a rectangular lattice of two-way streets; the reference world for tests and the TR 36.885 urban grid cols 6, rows 6, block_x_m/block_y_m 120, lanes_per_direction 1, signalised false, cycle_s 60, amber_s 3, ew_green_share 0.5, crossings, block_buildings, rsu_at_junctions, corner_radius_m world/source/procedural-radial spokes from a central plaza crossed by ring roads arms 6, rings 6, ring_spacing_m 120, dropout 0, signalised world/source/procedural-random an irregular network grown by random attachment, reproducible from its seed iterations 150, min_distance_m 80, max_distance_m 250, seed 1, min_angle_deg 45

Every parameter with its source: model parameters. The random generator is the only one that draws numbers, from one declared stream.

items.title: Buildings, terrain and vegetation
items.text:
Layer Settings Notes Buildings world.buildings.enabled, keep_holes, metres_per_level footprints from OSM with heights from tags; metres_per_level (the building:levels rule) is marked todo-calibrate. Buildings obstruct radio links Terrain world.terrain.dem, world.terrain.drape a DEM raster resampled bilinearly onto the world grid, voids filled from the nearest sample and counted. drape: true lifts every lane point, junction, building, site and signal head onto it (and changes the world hash) Vegetation world.vegetation keeps OSM woods, tree rows and single trees as a layer; radio.channel_model.foliage charges the ITU-R P.833 excess loss through it

DEM formats (crates/v2xw-world/src/dem.rs): SRTM .hgt (NASA SRTMGL1 one-degree tiles, corner read from the file name) and ESRI/USGS ASCII grid (.asc), the path for Copernicus GLO-30 after gdal_translate -of AAIGrid. Without a DEM every height is 0 and existing world hashes are unchanged. scenarios/real-world/portland-hills.yaml is the worked example, on worlds/dem/portland-downtown.asc (provenance in worlds/dem/portland-downtown.md).

items.title: Provenance and the cache
items.text:
Every world carries a provenance record: the source kind and id, the source box, the import date (from the scenario, never a clock, and excluded from the world hash), tool versions, projection and origin, the transformations applied, each layer's licence and counts of what was dropped. Worlds built from OpenStreetMap carry the ODbL attribution.

world.cache names a directory: the world is read from <key>.v2xwworld there when present, imported and written there when not. The key hashes the world section and the source files' contents, so an edited extract is a different world. The cached form round-trips exactly, so a cached run is the same run; a corrupt entry is re-imported, never an error.

items.title: Other data under worlds/
items.text: Path What worlds/fetch-gtfs.sh <city> [YYYYMMDD] download a GTFS feed, clip it to the box and one service day with v2xw-demand gtfs-clip, into worlds/cache/<city>.gtfs/ (Traffic demand) worlds/fetch-lust.sh rebuild the committed LuST subsection worlds/sumo/lust-veremi-sub.net.xml from a pinned commit and check its digest worlds/sumo/ committed SUMO networks and route files for the interop scenarios worlds/validation/*.json world-validation baselines for world_report --baseline worlds/cache/ git-ignored: extracts, GTFS feeds, cached worlds

items.title: Metric catalogue
items.text:
Every metric this build can measure: 172 definitions, generated from the MetricDef each provider publishes. A scenario selects metrics with its metrics: list (Metrics and outputs); each section below says which selection installs its metrics. Visibility gt means the metric is computed from ground truth that no node could observe, node that a node could compute it from what it received, and node-and-gt that it joins both. A health band, where a metric has one, is what v2xw compare and the Studio judge a value against.

Reading a row

Aggregation is how observations in a window are reduced. Min samples is the count below which a window reports insufficient instead of a value. Does not account for is what the definition deliberately leaves out.

Section Metrics Core metrics (all) 84 Credential and privacy metrics (all, security path) 4 Application metrics (all, applications enabled) 4 Energy and emissions (energy) 25 Signing overhead (signing) 29 Traffic control (traffic) 5 Detection scores (detection-scores) 8 Surrogate safety measures (ssm) 9 Runtime diagnostics (library only) 4

items.text:
The distribution of sampled actor accelerations over the window.

Field Value Unit m/s² Aggregation distribution Visibility gt Dimensions t Grid (quantum) 0.001 Min samples 30

Does not account for:

  • the same time-weighting bias as speed
  • jerk, which the kinematics channel does not carry

items.title: air_bytes_per_payload_byte
items.text:
Octets on the air per octet of application payload: how many bytes the air carries for each byte the application wanted to send.

Field Value Unit B/B Aggregation ratio: Σ octets on the air / Σ application payload octets Visibility node Dimensions t, msg_type Grid (quantum) 0.0001 Min samples 1

Does not account for:

  • frames with no payload/envelope split
  • the PHY preamble and tail, which are air time

items.title: airtime_per_node
items.text:
Transmitted air time per node, divided by the window's length. With no dimension, the mean over the nodes that transmitted in the window.

Field Value Unit ms/s Aggregation rate Visibility node Dimensions t, node Grid (quantum) 0.001 Min samples 1 Better lower (standard basis) Healthy within the 1 % duty cycle the relaxed DCC state allows Caution 10.0: above 10 ms/s: more than the relaxed DCC state's 1 % duty cycle Unhealthy 30.0: above 30 ms/s: past the 3 % per-station duty-cycle ceiling Band source ETSI TS 102 687 V1.2.1 reactive DCC Relaxed state (T_on 1 ms per T_off 100 ms, 1 %); EN 302 571 / TS 102 687 adaptive δ_max 0.03 (3 % = 30 ms/s)

Does not account for:

  • receive-side occupancy
  • inter-frame spacing and backoff, which are not transmitted time

items.title: aoi
items.text:
Age of information: how old, on average over time, the freshest message a receiver holds from each neighbour is — over the vehicles truly within 100 m that it has heard (SAE J2945/1's vPERRange; Kaul et al.'s system age), integrated exactly between mobility steps over the pairs within range at each step. Broken down at 100 m and 300 m, and all: every link's sawtooth but a VRU device's, integrated exactly between its deliveries, whatever the distance, which far links that rarely deliver dominate. Vehicles only: pedestrians' and riders' devices beacon at their own, lower rates, so vehicles' age about them within 100 m is the class vru sample.

Field Value Unit ms Aggregation ratio: Σ age × time / Σ time Visibility node-and-gt Dimensions t, radius, class Grid (quantum) 0.001 Min samples 1 Source Kaul, Gruteser, Rai, Kenney, IEEE SECON 2011; Kaul, Yates, Gruteser, IEEE INFOCOM 2012 (paper) Better lower (standard basis) Healthy what receivers know is under three message intervals old Caution 300.0: above 300 ms: receivers' picture is three or more 10 Hz intervals old Unhealthy 600.0: above 600 ms: older than the longest gap J2945/1 congestion control allows Band source SAE J2945/1 10 Hz BSM and vMaxITT 600 ms (Ahmad et al., IEEE TVT 68(3) 2019, Table I); three intervals is the run analyst's stale threshold

Does not account for:

  • neighbours in range never heard, or unheard for over aoi_restart_s: nar counts them
  • pseudonym changes: links are keyed by the true sender

items.title: aoi_peak
items.text:
Peak age of information: the age of a receiver's information about a sender just before a new message from it arrives.

Field Value Unit ms Aggregation distribution Visibility node-and-gt Dimensions t Grid (quantum) 0.001 Min samples 30 Source Costa, Codreanu, Ephremides, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 62(4), 2016 (paper)

Does not account for:

  • the first message on a link, which has no predecessor
  • links restarted after a silence longer than aoi_restart_s
  • links farther than 100 m at the delivery

items.title: cbr
items.text:
Channel busy ratio as measured by the MAC: for 802.11p, the fraction of a 100 ms window with CCA busy above −85 dBm; for C-V2X, the TS 38.215 §5.1.27 / TS 36.214 definition. Reported as a distribution over the window's per-node measurements; each is a node's own measurement over its own window, so the distribution is reported whatever the node count, with that count.

Field Value Unit ratio Aggregation distribution Visibility node Dimensions t, channel Grid (quantum) 0.0001 Min samples 1 Source 3GPP TS 38.215 §5.1.27; TS 36.214 (standard) Better lower (standard basis) Healthy below 0.50: congestion control has nothing to do Caution 0.5: above 0.50: SAE J2945/1 congestion control is lowering power and message rate Unhealthy 0.68: above the 0.68 ETSI congestion target; vehicles will throttle their messages Band source ETSI TS 102 687 V1.2.1 §5.4 (adaptive DCC CBR_target 0.68); SAE J2945/1 vMinCBP 50 % (Ahmad et al., IEEE TVT 68(3) 2019, Table I)

Does not account for:

  • energy the receiver could not hear (a hidden terminal)
  • which node measured it: this is the distribution across nodes

items.title: cert_bytes_share
items.text:
The share of the security envelope's octets that are attached certificates rather than eight-octet digests — the price of the certificate-attachment policy.

Field Value Unit ratio Aggregation ratio: Σ attached-certificate octets / Σ envelope octets Visibility node Dimensions t, msg_type Grid (quantum) 0.0001 Min samples 1

Does not account for:
